Name: Ahura Mazda
Description: Ahura Mazda, the “Wise Lord,” is the supreme creator and principal object of worship in Zoroastrian tradition. In the Gathas he is addressed as a knowing and choosing divine being closely identified with wisdom, truth, and the ordering power of asha; later theology develops fuller accounts of his creation and cosmic opposition to evil. He should therefore be understood as both a personal deity and the source of an ethical-cosmic order, not merely as an abstract principle.

Name: Angra Mainyu
Description: Angra Mainyu is the destructive or hostile spirit of Zoroastrian tradition. In the Gathas he is opposed primarily to Spenta Mainyu within the drama of moral choice; in later Zoroastrian cosmogony, as Ahriman, he becomes the cosmic adversary of Ohrmazd and produces destructive counter-creations, demons, disease, and death. The entry therefore distinguishes the earlier ethical opposition from the more fully personified dualism of later theology.
Historic-Mythic Status Tags: Mythical, Symbolic, Doctrinal/Canonical, Archetypal, Contested, Composite
Neumann Stages Tags: Ego Collapse, Descent into the Underworld, Battle with the Dragon

Name: Aša Vahišta
Description: Aša Vahišta, “Best Truth” or “Best Righteousness,” is one of the Amesha Spentas and personifies the right order of reality. Asha includes truth, justice, correct ritual, and the proper structure of the cosmos rather than functioning as an impersonal law that stands above the divine world. In later Zoroastrian tradition Aša Vahišta is especially associated with fire, through which truth and purity become ritually visible.
Historic-Mythic Status Tags: Symbolic, Concept, Doctrinal/Canonical, Archetypal, Devotional, Composite
Neumann Stages Tags: Mythic Ordering of Reality, Initiation
Category: Amesha Spenta of Truth and Order

Name: Spenta Mainyu
Description: Spenta Mainyu is the “Beneficent Spirit,” the life-promoting and creative orientation opposed to Angra Mainyu in the Gathas. Its relationship to Ahura Mazda is interpreted differently across Zoroastrian sources and scholarship: it can appear as Ahura Mazda’s active spirit, a mode of his beneficent agency, or a distinct member of the primordial opposition. The concept expresses growth, creation, truth-directed choice, and the increase of life.

Name: Mithra
Description: Mithra is an Indo-Iranian deity whose name is connected with contract, covenant, agreement, and reciprocal obligation. In the Avesta he is an all-seeing guardian of oaths, a protector of social and political order, a warrior patron, and a deity associated with dawn, daylight, and wide pastures. He was increasingly identified with the sun in later Iranian tradition, but he was not originally identical with the solar disk. Roman Mithras drew on Iranian names and motifs, yet Roman Mithraism was not simply an unchanged continuation of the Iranian cult.

Name: Vohu Manah
Description: Vohu Manah, “Good Mind” or “Good Purpose,” is one of the Amesha Spentas. It represents the capacity to recognize and choose truth, linking ethical thought, intention, and action. In the Gathas Vohu Manah can also mediate encounter with Ahura Mazda; in later tradition it is associated with beneficent animal creation, especially cattle. The figure is both personified divinity and moral faculty rather than merely an abstract rule of cognition.

Name: Spenta Ārmaiti
Description: Spenta Ārmaiti, commonly rendered “Holy Devotion,” is one of the Amesha Spentas. In the Gathas she expresses reverent commitment, right-minded submission, and the patient realization of truth; later Zoroastrian tradition associates her closely with the earth and its proper cultivation. She therefore joins an ethical disposition with the material world that humans are responsible for protecting and sustaining.

Name: Mašya
Description: Mašya is the first human male in the developed Zoroastrian cosmogony preserved chiefly in Middle Persian texts. He and Mašyānā grow from a plant that emerges from the seed of the primordial man Gayōmard, become the ancestors of humanity, and initially fall into error by crediting the Evil Spirit with creation. The narrative belongs primarily to later systematic cosmogony, even though it may preserve older Iranian material; it should not be treated as a securely dated early-Avestan biography.

Name: Mašyānā
Description: Mašyānā is the first human female in the developed Zoroastrian cosmogony preserved chiefly in Middle Persian texts. Together with Mašya, she grows from the plant produced by Gayōmard’s seed, becomes an ancestor of humankind, and participates in humanity’s first mistaken attribution of creation to the Evil Spirit. Her story combines fertility, kinship, moral choice, and the vulnerability of embodied human life, but its surviving full form is late rather than securely Old Avestan.

Name: Harahvaitī
Description: Harahvaitī is both an Iranian sacred river-name and the name associated with the historical region later known as Arachosia, centered around the Kandahar and Arghandab area. In Avestan religious geography the name also participates in the imagery of a great life-giving river connected with the waters of the world. It is therefore best treated as a sacred river-land and a partially personified geographical concept, not as an independently documented goddess with a full mythology.

Name: Haoma
Description: Haoma is simultaneously the name of a sacred plant, the ritual drink pressed from it, and the divinity or living force associated with the plant. The rite has a close Indo-Iranian parallel in Vedic Soma and became embedded in the Zoroastrian Yasna liturgy, where Haoma is praised for vitality, strength, fertility, and religious insight. The plant’s precise botanical identity and the extent of any intoxicating or visionary effect remain disputed, so the entry does not define Haoma simply as an entheogen.

Name: Āθravan
Description: Āθravan is an Avestan designation for a priestly function or class, not the name of an individual priest. The role belongs to the ritual personnel responsible for maintaining worship, recitation, sacrifice, and religious continuity. Although the word has often been linked to ātar, “fire,” that etymology is uncertain, and an āθravan should not automatically be reduced to a specialized fire-priest. The entry is retained as an institutional religious figure because the dataset also includes personified offices and concepts.

Name: Ātar
Description: Ātar is sacred fire understood both as a material element and as a divine presence within Zoroastrian worship. Fire illuminates ritual space, receives offerings, represents purity, and is closely linked with Asha, but it is not worshipped as an idol or as a simple Persian duplicate of the Vedic god Agni. Later fire temples institutionalized the maintenance of consecrated fires, while domestic and ritual fire had already occupied a central place in Iranian religious life.

Name: Aži Sruvara
Description: Aži Sruvara is a particular dragon or monstrous serpent in Iranian heroic tradition, remembered as an enemy slain by Kərəsāspa. The surviving references do not justify presenting him as a primordial pre-moral chaos principle or as the ancestor from which Aži Dahāka developed. He belongs instead to the wider Avestan pattern in which heroic figures establish order by overcoming specific destructive monsters.

Name: Jamshid (Yima in Avestan)
Description: Yima is an Avestan golden-age king who enlarges the earth, preserves living beings in a protected enclosure during a catastrophic winter, possesses extraordinary royal glory, and later loses that glory after a transgression or false word. In Middle and New Persian tradition he becomes Jamshid, a great culture-king credited with crafts, social organization, prosperity, and Nowruz, whose pride eventually causes his fall. The entry combines these related but historically layered forms rather than treating every later Jamshid motif as part of the earliest Avestan account.

Name: Zahhāk (Aži Dahāka)
Description: Aži Dahāka is an Avestan dragon described with three heads, three mouths, and six eyes, created as a destructive enemy of the ordered world. Later Middle Persian and epic tradition transforms him into Zahhāk, a foreign tyrant with serpents growing from his shoulders, whose reign consumes the lives of the young. Thraētaona/Ferīdūn defeats and binds him; the association with Mount Damavand and the shoulder-serpent narrative belong especially to the later development of the myth.

Name: Ferīdūn (Thraētaona)
Description: Thraētaona is an Avestan hero who overcomes Aži Dahāka and restores the threatened order of the world. In Middle and New Persian tradition he becomes Ferīdūn, the king aided by Kāveh’s uprising who defeats Zahhāk and later divides his realm among his sons Salm, Tur, and Iraj. His figure therefore develops from dragon-conquering hero into a dynastic and tragic king whose division of the world generates later Iranian and Turanian conflict.

Name: Kāveh the Blacksmith
Description: Kāveh is the heroic blacksmith of the Shāhnāmeh and related Persian storytelling traditions. After Zahhāk’s agents take his children to feed the tyrant’s serpents, Kāveh rejects a declaration praising Zahhāk’s justice, raises his leather apron as a rebel standard, and helps rally support for Ferīdūn. The apron later becomes the legendary Derafsh-e Kāviān. Kāveh is a powerful symbol of resistance by an ordinary craftsman, but claims about his existence in a specific early oral period cannot be demonstrated securely.

Name: Anāhitā
Description: Anāhitā is the later name of the Iranian water goddess Arədvī Sūrā Anāhitā, praised in the Avesta as a vast, pure, life-increasing river and a powerful maiden who grants fertility, health, victory, and legitimate rule. Her historical cult appears to combine the Avestan river divinity with a western Iranian goddess called Anāhiti. Under Artaxerxes II she is named with Ahura Mazda and Mithra in royal inscriptions and becomes especially prominent in royal and temple cult.

Name: Verethragna (Bahram)
Description: Vərəθraγna, later Bahrām, is the Iranian divinity of victory and victorious force. Yašt 14 presents him appearing in ten forms, including wind, bull, horse, camel, boar, youth, bird of prey, ram, goat, and armed warrior. These transformations express adaptable power rather than trickery, and the deity became an important patron of warriors, travelers, kings, and sacred fires in later Iranian tradition.

Name: Manūčehr
Description: Manūčehr is a legendary Pishdadian king in Iranian traditional history and the Shāhnāmeh, not an early Kayanian ruler. He is the descendant of Iraj and avenges Iraj’s murder by defeating the lines of Salm and Tur, thereby restoring the Iranian branch of Ferīdūn’s divided inheritance. His reign marks the continuation of legitimate kingship after a dynastic blood-feud, but his precise date, birthplace, and historical existence are not recoverable.

Name: Siyāvaš
Description: Siyāvaš is the innocent prince of Iranian epic tradition whose virtue is tested when he passes through fire to disprove a false accusation. Alienated from his father Kay Kāvus, he seeks refuge in Turan, marries Farangis, and is eventually killed through the intrigues of Afrāsiāb’s court. His death demands vengeance and prepares the birth and mission of his son Kay Khosrow. Later traditions, especially in Central Asia, developed cultic and local associations around the martyred prince.

Name: Kai Khosrow (Haosravah)
Description: Kavi Haosravah is an Avestan Kayanian ruler celebrated for defeating the Turanian enemy Fraŋrasyan. In Persian epic he becomes Kay Khosrow, son of Siyāvaš and Farangis, who avenges his father, defeats Afrāsiāb, rules justly, and finally relinquishes kingship before disappearing into a sacred or mysterious withdrawal. The figure joins an Avestan royal hero with the later epic ideal of a warrior-king capable of renouncing power.

Name: Rostam
Description: Rostam is the central champion of the Iranian epic cycle, especially associated with Zabulistan and Sistan. He protects successive Iranian kings, completes the Seven Labors, defeats monsters and rival warriors, and repeatedly rescues a throne whose rulers are often less reliable than he is. His strength is joined to tragic limitation: he unknowingly kills his son Sohrāb and later kills Esfandiyār under impossible political pressure. Rostam is not securely attested as a named hero in the surviving Avesta; his fullest form belongs to the later epic tradition.

Name: Kay Qobād
Description: Kay Qobād is the legendary founder of the Kayanian dynasty in Persian traditional history. When Iran lacks an effective king, Rostam brings him from the Alborz region and places him on the throne, beginning the Kayanian line. His significance lies primarily in dynastic transition and restored legitimacy rather than in an independently developed personal mythology. The setting and chronology are epic conventions, not recoverable historical biography.

Name: Sohrāb
Description: Sohrāb is the son of Rostam and Tahmīna in the Shāhnāmeh. Raised in Samangan and drawn into Afrāsiāb’s campaign against Iran, he hopes to find his unknown father and replace the existing rulers with Rostam, but the two meet in combat without recognizing one another. Rostam mortally wounds him and learns his identity only afterward. The episode is fundamentally a tragedy of concealment, divided loyalties, and failed recognition, not a narrative designed simply to prove Iranian supremacy over Turan.

Name: Goštāsp (Vištāspa)
Description: Vištāspa appears in the Gathic and Avestan tradition as the royal patron who supports Zarathustra and his religious community. His precise historical identity, realm, and date remain uncertain. Later Zoroastrian and Persian epic tradition transforms him into Goštāsp, a Kayanian king whose conversion establishes the new faith at court and whose conflicts with his son Esfandiyār become central to the epic cycle. The entry distinguishes the possible historical patron from the later legendary monarch.

Name: Zarathustra
Description: Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, is the founding prophet of the Mazdayasnian tradition and the figure to whom the Gathas are attributed. He reoriented inherited Iranian religion around devotion to Ahura Mazda, the opposition of asha and druj, moral responsibility, and the cosmic significance of human choice. His date and homeland remain heavily disputed: proposals range broadly within the second and first millennia BCE, and an eastern Iranian setting is more defensible than a precise birthplace at Bactra. Later texts greatly expand his biography beyond what can be recovered from the Gathas.

Name: Esfandiyār
Description: Esfandiyār, corresponding to Avestan Spəntōδāta, is the warrior son of Vištāspa/Goštāsp and a champion associated with the defense and spread of the Zoroastrian religion. In the Shāhnāmeh he completes seven trials, rescues his sisters, and is protected by a near-invulnerable body, yet his father sends him to compel Rostam’s submission. Rostam kills him with a specially prepared tamarisk arrow. The conflict supports several political and ethical interpretations, but it should not be reduced to a proven historical struggle between priests and an older warrior class.

Name: Achaemenes
Description: Achaemenes is the eponymous ancestor from whom Darius I and later rulers derived the name and antiquity of the Achaemenid dynasty. He appears in Darius’s royal genealogy as the father of Teispes, but no securely contemporary record independently confirms his reign or biography. He may preserve a historical clan ancestor, a dynastic construction, or both. The approximate date and location are genealogical reconstructions rather than verified life data.

Name: Cyrus the Great
Description: Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great, founded the Achaemenid Empire by defeating the Median king Astyages, conquering Lydia, and taking Babylon in 539 BCE. He generally ruled through existing institutions and local elites, restored displaced cult images in Babylonia, and became associated in biblical tradition with the return of Judean exiles and the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple. His reputation for ideal kingship grew in several later traditions, but modern descriptions should distinguish imperial pragmatism from the simplified image of a uniquely modern humanitarian ruler. He died during an eastern campaign around 530 BCE.

Name: Cambyses II
Description: Cambyses II, son and successor of Cyrus the Great, ruled the Achaemenid Empire from 530 to 522 BCE. He conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, assumed pharaonic titles, and attempted to incorporate Egyptian institutions into Achaemenid rule. Hostile Greek traditions portray him as mad and sacrilegious, but those stories must be weighed against Egyptian and administrative evidence. He died while returning from Egypt after news that Bardiya—or a man claiming to be Bardiya—had seized power, producing the succession crisis from which Darius I emerged.

Name: Darius I
Description: Darius I ruled from 522 to 486 BCE after overthrowing the ruler identified in his inscriptions as the usurper Gaumāta and defeating widespread rebellions. He reorganized taxation and provincial administration, developed royal roads and communications, issued the gold daric, expanded imperial building at Susa and Persepolis, and extended Persian power toward the Indus and southeastern Europe. His inscriptions repeatedly credit Ahuramazda and condemn the Lie, but whether his religion should be identified without qualification with later normative Zoroastrianism remains debated. He was buried at Naqsh-e Rustam.

Name: Xerxes I
Description: Xerxes I, son of Darius I and Atossa, ruled from 486 to 465 BCE. He suppressed unrest in Egypt and Babylonia, continued major construction at Persepolis, and led the large invasion of Greece in 480 BCE, winning at Thermopylae before the Persian fleet was defeated at Salamis and the land campaign ended after Plataea and Mycale. His royal inscriptions invoke Ahuramazda and emphasize legitimate kingship and obedience. Greek literary portrayals of him as an archetypal eastern despot are culturally charged sources rather than neutral biography. He was assassinated in a court conspiracy.

Name: Esther
Description: Esther is the central Jewish heroine of the Book of Esther, a narrative set at the Achaemenid court in Susa. Concealing her identity after becoming queen, she risks approaching King Ahasuerus, exposes Haman’s plan to destroy the Jews, and helps secure their survival; the story provides the literary foundation for Purim. Ahasuerus is commonly identified with Xerxes I, but Esther herself is not independently attested in Persian records, and the book is a literary work composed after the events it depicts. Proposed links between her name and Ishtar remain debated.

Name: Artaxerxes II
Description: Artaxerxes II Mnemon ruled from 405/404 to 359/358 BCE, the longest reign of any Achaemenid king. He defeated the rebellion of his brother Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa, reasserted Persian influence over the Greek world through the King’s Peace, confronted repeated revolts and unsuccessful campaigns against Egypt, and nevertheless preserved the empire across a long and difficult reign. His inscriptions are the first Achaemenid royal texts to name Anāhitā and Mithra alongside Ahuramazda. This is important evidence for royal cult, but it does not justify calling him straightforwardly a “devout Zoroastrian” in the later confessional sense.

Name: Khshathra Vairya
Description: Khshathra Vairya, more precisely Xšaθra Vairya, means “Desirable Dominion” and is one of the Amesha Spentas. It represents the ideal exercise of divine and human power in accordance with truth, including protection of the weak and the establishment of a just order. Later Zoroastrian tradition associates it with metal and the stone or metallic sky. The concept is not simply a defense of existing hierarchy; it is a standard by which authority is judged.

Name: Haurvatat
Description: Haurvatat, “Wholeness” or “Completeness,” is one of the Amesha Spentas. It represents health, integrity, and the perfected condition of creation, and in later Zoroastrian tradition is associated with water. Haurvatat is frequently paired with Ameretat, immortality, so that completeness and enduring life become complementary dimensions of salvation and the final renovation of the world.

Name: Ameretat
Description: Ameretat, “Immortality,” is one of the Amesha Spentas. It expresses deathless life and the enduring fulfillment of creation, and in later Zoroastrian tradition is associated with plants. Ameretat is regularly paired with Haurvatat, wholeness, linking nourishment, health, completeness, and immortality within ritual practice and the eschatological renewal of the world.
